Official Scope + Assigned Resources

1. Describe the pathogenesis of HIV infection.
2. Recognize signs and symptoms of each stage of HIV infection.
3. Identify risk factors, presentation, and treatment of common HIV-associated opportunistic infections.
4. Discuss the role of CD4+ cells in prevention of opportunistic infections and thresholds for pharmacologic prophylaxis.
Assigned resources
ScholarRx · Human immunodeficiency virusScholarRx · Neurologic complications related to HIVAssigned Nature Reviews HIV primer
Best mental map: HIV entry/replication → CD4 loss and progressive immune dysfunction → AIDS definition → CD4-linked opportunistic infections. For the OIs, pair threshold + hallmark presentation + diagnostic clue + treatment/prophylaxis.

Slides 3–14 · HIV Pathogenesis, Progression & Diagnosis

Life-cycle sequence

Binding → fusion → reverse transcription → integration → replication → assembly → budding. The deck’s life-cycle figure is the core sequence to know.

Early pathophysiology

The deck depicts early viral replication increasing while CD4 T cells and gut barrier function decrease. HIV then establishes chronic infection with progressive immune dysfunction.

Slide 4. Faculty life-cycle figure: binding, fusion, reverse transcription, integration, replication, assembly, and budding.

CD4

Transmembrane glycoprotein on helper T cells; normally interacts with MHC on APCs and is the major HIV binding site.

Coreceptors

Chemokine GPCRs aid HIV binding and entry. The faculty binding figure labels CCR5/CXCR4 in the entry sequence.

CCR5 Δ32

Homozygous deletion → HIV resistance in the deck; heterozygous → slower progression. The slide also notes increased symptomatic West Nile risk.

Non-CD4 presentations shown: astrocyte-associated HIV neurocognitive disorder (HAND) and renal epithelial-cell HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN).
Slide 12. Progression graphic: acute viremia with early CD4 fall, partial immune control/set point, then gradual CD4 decline and later viral rebound into AIDS.

Elite controllers

The deck identifies ~1% of patients as elite controllers / long-term nonprogressors.

Diagnosis timing

The deck’s diagnostic figure places nucleic acid testing earliest, then p24/antigen-antibody detection, followed by later antibody responses. It explicitly notes that Western blot is no longer used for HIV diagnosis.

Slide 15 · AIDS Definition

AIDS = CD4 < 200 cells/mm³ OR an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection/condition.
AIDS-defining examples listed in the deckAdditional examples listed
Candida esophagitis · Pneumocystis pneumonia · cryptococcosis · histoplasmosis · cryptosporidiosis · CMV · TB · toxoplasmosis · NTM infectionHIV encephalopathy · Burkitt/immunoblastic/CNS lymphoma · PML · Kaposi sarcoma · recurrent Salmonella septicemia · HIV wasting · HSV >1 month
Threshold trap: the deck does not require CD4 <200 if an AIDS-defining condition is present. Either criterion is enough.

Slides 16–18 · Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia

Threshold + prophylaxis

CD4 <200 cells/µL or <14%. Prophylaxis options listed: TMP-SMX, atovaquone, dapsone, inhaled pentamidine.

Diagnosis

Bronchoalveolar lavage; PCR; Giemsa and methenamine silver stains; DFA. LDH >500 and 1,3-β-D-glucan are labeled less reliable.

Moderate–severe PCP: room-air PaO₂ <70 mmHg OR A–a gradient ≥35 mmHg → TMP-SMX + corticosteroids.
Slide 17. PCP threshold, prophylaxis, diagnosis, and moderate–severe classification criteria.
Alternatives: mild disease options include dapsone, primaquine + clindamycin, or atovaquone; moderate–severe alternatives include primaquine + clindamycin or IV pentamidine. The deck requires G6PD testing before dapsone/primaquine.

Slides 19–25 · Toxoplasmosis, CNS Lymphoma & PML

Cerebral toxoplasmosis

Usually reactivation. Imaging usually shows multiple lesions with a predilection for the basal ganglia; MRI > CT.

CNS lymphoma

Linked to EBV. Headache, seizure, focal deficits; enhancing lesions with edema; deck uses CSF EBV PCR for diagnosis.

PML

JC virus, usually CD4 <50. White-matter demyelination → gait disturbance, confusion, homonymous hemianopsia. Treat underlying HIV.

Slide 21. Toxoplasmosis imaging: typically multiple lesions with basal-ganglia predilection; MRI is preferred to CT.
Toxo diagnosis: consistent clinical/radiographic picture + Toxoplasma IgG + response to therapy can support presumptive diagnosis. CSF PCR is highly specific (96–100%) but poorly sensitive (~50%); biopsy is reserved for failure of empiric therapy.
Toxoplasma prophylaxisPreferred treatmentStopping prophylaxis in deck
CD4 <100 + IgG+: TMP-SMX; alternatives include dapsone+pyrimethamine+leucovorin or atovaquonePyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin OR TMP-SMXCD4 >200 for >3 months + HIV RNA suppression, OR CD4 100–200 with suppression for at least 3–6 months
Slide 25. PML: JC-virus white-matter disease, generally at CD4 <50.

Slides 26–33 · Cryptococcus & MAC

Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii

Deck presentations: meningitis, pneumonia, cryptococcemia, skin lesions. Diagnostic workup: cryptococcal antigen, PCR, culture; India ink is shown as the classic morphology image.

Cryptococcal therapy sequence

Induction: liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine ×2 weeks → consolidation: fluconazole 800 mg daily ×8 weeks → maintenance: fluconazole 200 mg daily for 1 year from induction.

Slide 28. India ink image of encapsulated Cryptococcus.
Ozzy found the CNS OI aisle. Multiple basal-ganglia lesions = toxoplasmosis; white-matter demyelination = PML; meningitis + India ink = Cryptococcus.

MAC pattern

Ubiquitous environmental organism; CD4 <50. Disseminated disease can produce anemia, fever, night sweats, diarrhea, weight loss, abdominal pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly.

MAC treatment

Backbone: clarithromycin or azithromycin + ethambutol. Add rifabutin in severe disease; the slide lists several possible optional fourth drugs.

Slide 32. MAC prophylaxis is not recommended if suppressive ART is being started. Indication in the deck: CD4 <50 plus no ART / no fully suppressive option; rule out disseminated MAC first.
MAC prophylaxis trap: do not memorize “CD4 <50 = automatically prophylax.” The deck explicitly conditions prophylaxis on ART status and says to rule out disseminated MAC first.

Slides 34–37 · Kaposi Sarcoma + GI Opportunistic Infections

Kaposi sarcoma

HHV-8. Nontender hyperpigmented macular or nodular lesions, including oral mucosa and lymph nodes; up to 50% have visceral involvement.

Treatment in deck

T0: antiretrovirals alone. T1: antiretrovirals + liposomal doxorubicin.

Slide 35. AIDS Clinical Trials Group–style T/I/S staging: tumor extent, immune status, and systemic illness.
GI OIs listed: Cryptosporidium parvum, Giardia duodenalis, Microsporidium/Isospora (Cystoisospora belli), enteric pathogens, and CMV enteritis. The faculty questions specifically reinforce Cryptosporidium with watery diarrhea + sclerosing cholangitis in advanced HIV.

Last 60 Seconds

HIV entry = CD4 + coreceptor → RT → integration → replication/assembly/budding · AIDS = CD4 <200 OR defining condition · PCP <200 · Toxo <100 + IgG+ · MAC/PML usually <50 · PCP severe = PaO₂ <70 or A–a ≥35 → steroids · Toxo = multiple basal-ganglia lesions · PML = JC white matter · Crypto = CrAg/India ink; ampho+flucytosine → fluconazole · MAC = macrolide + ethambutol · Kaposi = HHV-8.
